articles.title: M11: The team behind Keely Hodgkinson's golden rise and pursuit of 800m world record
articles.summary: BBC Sport looks at the team behind Great Britain 800m star Keely Hodgkinson's golden rise and pursuit of a world record.
articles.body:
The Olympic champion and the world silver medallist over 800m embrace by the side of the track after surviving their latest brutal training session together during an east Manchester downpour.

A short while ago, Keely Hodgkinson lay flat out on the track.

Coach Trevor Painter, aware it may be some time before Hodgkinson can move again, places an opened umbrella beside his star athlete to shield her from the incessant rain, before running for cover.

It requires the assistance of two team-mates to eventually peel her off the ground.

Georgia Hunter Bell, meanwhile, uses the little energy she has left to take herself away to be sick.

Observing it all, Painter jokes he is mostly disappointed that relatively few of their team-mates have suffered the same fate on this occasion, when the cameras are rolling.

This is, after all, what it takes to be part of M11 Track Club, where the emphasis is on fun until the stopwatch starts.

Named after the postcode in which it is based, the near-30 strong international training group continue to create history under the guidance of the meticulous Painter and partner Jenny Meadows, a world medallist who has put herself through all the anguish she now oversees.

There is no doubt in the mind of Hodgkinson, winner of six global medals in as many years as a professional athlete, about the important role of this support system in her monumental achievements.

"I think it's everything," the 24-year-old Hodgkinson tells BBC Sport.

"I probably wouldn't be the person I am without it. We have a very fun approach to training, I love everybody in this group.

"Environment is everything. We have people from all around the world training here. We all get along really well, we're all respective of each other's journey, and we all know that if we want to continue being the best, we've got to train with the best.

European Athletics Championships: Key events, timetable & BBC coverage Published 17 August

European Athletics Championships: Key events, timetable & BBC coverage

The sense of community and camaraderie among individuals from around the globe is instantly evident as the team arrive and gather in a small room to begin their activation work and receive light physiotherapy.

Newest recruit Gaia Sabbatini, who has traded training in Rome to be here, is welcomed with happy birthday wishes and balloons - but there is a prevailing sense of apprehension among the athletes about what lies in store.

The miserable weather is the least of their worries, and it will not be long before the Italian is telling us all that she feels like she is "dying".

Painter might be the only one laughing and joking at that stage, but that is mostly founded in the knowledge that, by the time they are done here, they will each be sufficiently exhausted to know they are another step closer to realising their goals.

"I'm really passionate about the environment we've created," Painter says.

"There are a lot of friendships, it is like a family. But, when the time comes, you roll your sleeves up.

"There will be people bent over being sick and going to a very dark place during training, but the friendships and the fun that we have make it that little bit easier."

A lactic acid-inducing session comprising 400m intervals in early June signals the start of a specific 800m training block to prepare for the summer's major targets.

That Hodgkinson was able to run a British 800m record in Stockholm just a few days before, having not begun her event-specific work, was cause for significant optimism, albeit she was outshone by Swiss athlete Audrey Werro clocking the fastest time since the world record was set 43 years ago.

Despite the conditions, Painter informs us that Hodgkinson, perhaps motivated by that unexpected defeat, has outperformed all expectations. She has beaten her personal best splits for this session, going faster than times posted in the lead-up to an outstanding indoor season in which she captured world gold and the indoor 800m world record.

The M11 foundations were in place long before Hodgkinson's father suggested the group's now globally recognised title.

Painter, who boasts a background in rugby league and an impressive 47-second 400m time, has overseen Hodgkinson's development since she was 17. Before then, he coached Meadows to international success.

It has taken just two years for Meadows' vision of an official Manchester-based training group to become reality and earn a global reputation.

"I think everyone thought I was quite deluded. I had a vision of this happening, but I didn't quite know how we were going to achieve it," says Meadows.

"At first, when we would hear people from other nations talk about M11, I was almost like, 'oh my gosh, they've said M11'. It's almost like a project that I brought home from school, and people are talking about it.

"Now people know instantly: that's Jenny and Trevor, that's some of the best athletes in the world. You don't have to explain what M11 is. It's pretty incredible."

The process was undoubtedly accelerated by Hodgkinson's rise to Olympic gold, and further medals at Paris 2024 for team-mates Hunter Bell and Lewis Davey.

The sustained success on the track has allowed Painter and Meadows to expand the scale of their operation, with backing from big-name sponsors helping to add an assistant coach, track-side physiotherapist and dedicated physiologist.

"Back in the day, it was difficult because you're working on a shoestring budget, trying to make things happen," says Painter.

"But, as Keely comes along and does well, you get a little bit of help from here and there.

"Then, as more people come and we have more success, we can go back to the sponsors and they give us a little more. It pays for strength and conditioning support, nutrition support, trackside physiotherapy - all which keep the athletes healthy.

"If they're healthy, they can do their job of running as fast as they can."

Defiant Hodgkinson says home European title would mean as much as Olympic gold Published 9 August

Defiant Hodgkinson says home European title would mean as much as Olympic gold

Hunter Bell eyes ambitious sweep after Glasgow gold Published 31 July

Hunter Bell eyes ambitious sweep after Glasgow gold

The public-use SportCity track in the shadows of Manchester City's Premier League stadium, the occasional car park in Wigan, and the famous dirt track ascending 'hell hill' on South Africa training camps are humbling, no-nonsense settings for some of the world's top athletes to be honing their craft.

But they are very much in keeping with the values which Painter and Meadows have instilled in a group that continue to hit spectacular heights.

There are no egos among a carefully hand-picked selection of athletes who push each other on and, when needed, pick each other up.

The knock-on positive impact on athletic performance, in what is typically considered an individual sport, is at the heart of what Painter and Meadows have built - and why they continue to prioritise protecting that ecosystem.

"The team aspect is so powerful. It doesn't matter which athlete it is; if someone's having a bad day, there's always someone to put their arm around you or give you that little motivational comment that helps you back out of your mood," says Painter.

"We celebrate each and everybody's wins - and we suffer each and everyone's losses, pains and injuries.

"People who come into the squad, they look around and they see the Olympic champion on her hands and knees being sick, and the next minute she's getting ice poured over her. It's like, 'oh, right, that's normal, is it?'"

Despite social media evidence to the contrary, Painter pleads he is "not always the culprit" when it comes to the pouring of ice buckets.

As the group's pursuit of global titles and world records has gathered momentum, it has left no shortage of prospective athletes desperate to be invited in.

Painter and Meadows are inundated with applications from eager individuals via social media, email and in person, while sponsors Nike will also suggest athletes for their consideration.

Although most athletes on the circuit are known to them, Painter and Meadows are extremely thorough in their process of identifying those that are the right fit and will seek to gather information on any names which come their way.

If they appear suitable, and if they decide there is room for development, the M11 coaches will arrange an informal chat with the athlete, before inviting them to take part in a session and observe how they fit into the group.

"We look at where athletes are, what the trajectory is like, what they've done in the past," says Painter.

"Some athletes have done far too much as youngsters. They've been pushed too hard and there's not much you can do to fix them. There's others that haven't done enough and you've got to work out how to take them from where they are to what I think they need to do.

"But character-wise is the most important factor because I'm going to get them to do some horrific things in training.

"Whether that's hill sessions or track sessions, there's no getting away from the pain.

"Those that are prepared to do that, and have fun along the way, are welcomed in. It's a long process, but we've got to protect the environment."

Painter and Meadows were crowned BBC Sports Personality Coach of the Year winners in 2024.

They remain resolutely modest when it comes to their own achievements, while the results continue to speak for themselves.

The demand for their attention is no surprise.

When Hodgkinson joined Painter, she could run 400m in around 57 seconds and 800m in two minutes and 4.26 seconds. Having lowered those personal bests to 51:14 and 1:54.33 respectively over seven years, she has established herself among the sport's leading stars.

Hunter Bell was in full-time work when she re-established contact with childhood coach Painter at the end of 2022, having not worn a pair of spikes for five years after falling out of love with the sport during her time on a track scholarship in the United States.

The 32-year-old has gone on to win six international medals, including Olympic bronze, world silver and the world indoor 1500m title.

Meadows famously joked "that ship has sailed" upon learning the former English schools champion had got back in touch with Painter.

But Hunter Bell is arguably as good a reference as Hodgkinson of Painter's talent for developing athletes, evident once again at this year's World Indoors when the pair celebrated their respective 800m and 1500m triumphs together on the track.

It is not only athletes who are desperate to join the project.

Some 180 applications were received for the role of physiologist alone, with Rachel McCormick willing to uproot her life from Australia to take the job.

Concerns held by Painter and Meadows over whether M11 was "going to be enough" for McCormick to justify the move across the world were soon dispelled.

"When I was applying for the job, I thought 'I didn't know there was a dream job out there, but this could genuinely be it'," says McCormick, who has published more than 50 research papers.

Having joined in late 2025, McCormick has taken time to pore over data from each athlete, measuring how they respond during and after sessions, and how well they recover and adapt, and is now in the first season of using that to feed into training.

"This is an incredibly elite group, and Trevor and Jenny have a history of success, so I haven't exactly come in here and revolutionised anything," McCormick says.

"What I've been trying to look for are the small wins. Where can I get the biggest gain without changing or drastically shifting anything that they're already doing?"

The fine details in which McCormick specialises were not as readily available to Meadows during her own career on the track.

Meadows says their new team member's credentials "absolutely petrified" her and Painter initially.

Today, McCormick is busy chasing after athletes to take blood lactate levels in between their efforts, and she will continue to process and analyse them long after the session has ended. A smart ring, worn on the finger of the athletes, assists in monitoring their data away from the track.

The training methods at M11, centred on gruelling intensity in sessions and the utilisation of cross-training to aid recovery, are different to anything McCormick says she has seen before. Her readings back that up.

"Middle distance is really interesting in that there are so many ways to train for the events," says McCormick.

"Georgia and Keely are very different athletes, yet in the 800 they're within a second of each other. I'd like to think that the data I'm collecting will give us insights that most people don't have."

Meadows says: "We might think athletes are adapting to training a certain way because we know what the stopwatch says, but Rachel can give us in-depth data about that and help us to make smarter decisions.

"We are hunting for a world record with Keely in the 800m, Georgia might decide to double up on events at the next Olympics, so it's asking 'how do we get all of that right?'."

There is perhaps no greater indication of the strength of the environment which Painter and Meadows have fostered than the handling of last year's World Championships in Tokyo.

Hodgkinson, fighting to recover from two hamstring tears earlier in the year, was joined by the ever-improving Hunter Bell in setting sights on the same 800m gold.

It was a potentially awkward scenario that would end with two medals - and the two M11 athletes singing karaoke together late into the night.

With both set up to achieve success based on the best individual plan for them, Hodgkinson and Hunter Bell were able to proceed as normal, even performing warm-up drills together in the corridor of their hotel to escape the stifling humidity outside.

The pair have become close friends since Hunter Bell returned to the sport, and closer still following their shared experience in Tokyo.

That is something Hodgkinson feels is "the opposite of what a lot of people might think would happen".

Despite being overhauled and pipped to silver by her team-mate in a dramatic finish, Hodgkinson celebrated together with Hunter Bell on the track.

"I feel like we're like sisters," says Hunter Bell.

"Obviously, when we step on the start line, we both want to win. But day-to-day, it's just like being with your best mates and it allows us all to train really hard."

That is a sentiment echoed unequivocally by Hodgkinson, who said: "We have a great relationship. In a weird way, [competing against each another] actually made us better friends.

"I'm just grateful to have her to train with because I think it genuinely pushes us on to be better and better."

But it all comes back to the coaches who have led them here.

"Together they're a really good guiding force, but you do see them like family, like second parents," says Hunter Bell.

"I have to give Jen and Trev a lot of credit for the culture that they have created."

articles.title: Robot Breaks Usain Bolt's 100m Record on Video at Olympics-like World Humanoid Robot Games in China
articles.summary: It took 17 years to find anything in the world that can run the 100 meters faster than Usain Bolt, but a humanoid robot created in China finally did it.
articles.body:
It took 17 years to find anything in the world that can run the 100 meters faster than Usain Bolt, but a humanoid robot created in China finally did it.

A humanoid robot ran the 100 meters in 9.39 seconds at the World Humanoid Robot Games on Saturday, breaking the human world record of 9.58 seconds set by Bolt at the 2009 World Championships.

That wasn't the only time one of the robots surpassed a world record set by a human.

Per Achmad Ibrahim and Chan Ho-Him of the Associated Press, a humanoid robot hit 2.88 meters in the standing high jump. The human record is 2.45 meters set by Cuba's Javier Sotomayor in 1993.

Ibrahim and Ho-Him noted both of the robots that broke the records are from X-Humanoid, which is based in Beijing.

The World Humanoid Robot Games are an Olympic-like event featuring humanoid robots. Saturday marks the first day of the 2026 Games, which are scheduled to run through Aug. 26.

After having more than 280 teams from various universities and private companies in 2025, the field has expanded significantly this with 666 teams and 2,056 robots competing.

There are 30 competitive sporting events taking place over the five days. Track and field, dance, wushu and gymnastics are among the disciplines in the competition.

articles.title: After Breaking Usain Bolt's Record, Robot Breaks Another Human Track Feat at World Humanoid Games
articles.summary: The machines have claimed another world record in track and field.
articles.body:
The machines have claimed another world record in track and field.

The robot Tiangong ran the 400 meters in 38.15 seconds in the World Humanoid Robot Games.

That would smash the mark set by South Africa's Wayde van Niekerk (43.03 seconds) during the 2016 Summer Olympics.

Usain Bolt's 100-meter record went down earlier in the weekend.

It wasn't the only human achievement the robots managed to best, either.

articles.title: Usain Bolt & Girlfriend Kasi Bennett Get Engaged, Latest Photos, Videos and Details on Diamond Ring
articles.summary: Olympic sprinting legend Usain Bolt proposed to longtime girlfriend Kasi Bennett during his 40th birthday celebration on Friday, per multiple reports.
articles.body:
Olympic sprinting legend Usain Bolt proposed to longtime girlfriend Kasi Bennett during his 40th birthday celebration on Friday, per multiple reports .

The couple has been dating since 2013 and have three children together.

Bolt is considered the greatest sprinter of all time, with eight Olympic gold medals and world records in the 100-meter dash (9.58 seconds) and 200-meter dash (19.19 seconds).

articles.title: Hockey World Cup: Argentina dash Indiaâs slim semifinal hopes
articles.summary: Hockey News: Thirty-six seconds. That was all it took for Indiaâs threadbare hope of reaching the FIH World Cup semifinals to disappear.At the Wagener Hockey Stadi.
articles.body: Thirty-six seconds. That was all it took for Indiaâs threadbare hope of reaching the FIH World Cup semifinals to disappear.At the Wagener Hockey Stadium in Amstelveen, Netherlands, Argentina exposed Indiaâs defensive frailties and ended Harmanpreet Singh and his menâs semifinal aspirations with a 5-3 win in their final Stage 2 match on Monday.Saturdayâs 1-3 defeat to cohosts Netherlands had all but extinguished Indiaâs hopes of a podium finish. Argentina, however, drove the final nail into the coffin.Lacklustre defending, poor marking and possession that produced little end product summed up Indiaâs evening. For all their control of the ball, they struggled to keep Argentinaâs attackers at bay.The only consolation was that two of Indiaâs three goals came from open play. But seven penalty corners went begging, a statistic that once again underlined their struggles.Barely had India settled into the contest when Joaquin Toscani punished a defensive error. Jarmanpreet Singh failed to intercept a ball across the goalmouth and Toscani made no mistake, firing Argentina ahead.Argentina kept the pressure on and doubled their advantage. Nicolas della Torre converted the ir second penalty corner in the sixth minute, exposing another lapse in Indiaâs defensive organisation.Sukhjeet Singh gave India a lifeline in the 10th minute, finishing from close range.India had opportunities to draw level in the second quarter but failed to take them.Argentina restored their two-goal advantage when Tomas Domeneâs 33rd minute reverse hit beat goalkeeper HS Mohith.Domene then completed his brace in the 45th minute, converting a penalty stroke. Lucas Toscani added Argentinaâs fifth, leaving Indian shoulders sagging.Sukhjeet pulled one back in the 58th minute before Hardil Singh reduced the margin further a minute later.India will now play Belgium in the 7-8 classification match.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: âSave womenâs HILâ: Indian hockey stars make emotional plea as league faces uncertain future
articles.summary: Hockey News: NEW DELHI: Indiaâs women hockey players have made an emotional appeal to save the Womenâs Hockey India League (HIL), insisting that the competition ha.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Indiaâs women hockey players have made an emotional appeal to save the Womenâs Hockey India League (HIL), insisting that the competition has played a crucial role in building the confidence of a young side that is on the brink of its best-ever World Cup finish since 1974.With 11 World Cup debutants in the squad, India have suffered only one defeat against Olympic champions the Netherlands and held Olympic silver medallists China to a 2-2 draw in their opening match. A goalless draw against Australia ended their hopes of reaching the semifinals, but India will now play for fifth and sixth place â a finish that would still be their best at the World Cup in 52 years.The players believe the Women's HIL has been central to their progress and fear its discontinuation could damage the pathway for the next generation.âHIL has benefited us a lotâVeteran midfielder Neha, who led Odisha Warriors to the inaugural HIL title in the 2024-25 season, stressed the importance of the league in giving young players access to a higher level of competition.âI think we have done our best to inspire girls in India to hold a hockey stick. People prefer their kids to play individual sports, but this should give them hope,â Neha told PTI.âIn the last two years, HIL for women has benefited us a lot. Junior and senior Nationals do not have this level of competition. Women's HIL has given us players like Baljeet, Sakshi and Rutuja, who are part of this World Cup team. For upcoming players also, we need this league. It should not be discontinued.âSalima Tete highlights talent pathwayCaptain Salima Tete also underlined how the league has helped widen India's talent pool and given emerging players a route into the national setup.âWe have many players from HIL in the Indian team. They get a chance to be selected for the national camp, which is an important opportunity for them,â she said.âThis is just the beginning for us and there is much more to achieve. For that, HIL is a must so that our talent pool is broadened and the girls get good exposure to handling the pressure of international hockey.ââHIL has given me confidenceâSakshi Rana, another player who has benefited from the league, said the experience of playing alongside established international stars helped her handle pressure on the biggest stage.âHIL has given me confidence, which was very useful in this tournament. It is about handling pressure. We have played alongside many veteran players like World Cup top scorer Yibbi Janssen and learnt a lot,â she said.Navneet Kaur said the league also helped younger players overcome the fear of facing established international stars.âWe have been playing HIL for the last two years and gained confidence from that. We have played with some of the biggest names in international hockey and after sharing the dressing room with them, the fear and hesitation was gone,â she said.âThat gave us self-belief. We often discuss that they are like us and we can beat them because we have played with them.âNavneet urges corporate sector to step inNavneet also urged franchises and corporate houses to step in as the women's league faces financial uncertainty.âWe have heard that a few teams are pulling out of the Women's HIL, but at a time when our performance graph is going up, we want to request them to support us. It will be a big setback for women's hockey and the future crop of players,â she said.âI request the Sports Ministry and Hockey India to save this league. I also request the corporate sector, which invests huge money in cricket, to support women's hockey.âOur league does not require that much money. It is not about money, we need exposure. Women's Hockey League should survive. We will do even better in the future,â added Navneet, who was player of the tournament last season with the Delhi team.Financial challenges threaten women's HILThe appeal comes as the revived women's HIL grapples with high operating costs, low broadcast and ticket revenues, delayed player payments and limited sponsorship interest. Franchise sources said the league is currently not commercially viable, with the cost of running both a men's and women's HIL team estimated at around Rs 10-12 crore, including an administrative fee of around Rs 1 crore. The women's franchise fee of Rs 2.5 crore, however, has been removed for the third season.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Un atleta de 92 años gana los 100 m del Mundial máster... ¡con 18.29!
articles.standfirst: Radnaa Tseren, de Mongolia, se impone en la final de la distancia en categoría M90
articles.summary: Radnaa Tseren, de Mongolia, se impone en la final de la distancia en categoría M90
articles.body: En 1962 Radnaa Tseren ingresó en el Instituto Nacional de Educación Física de Mongolia y ahí empezó a correr. Pocos años después, en 1966 y tras graduarse en la Universidad, comenzó a participar en carreras de corta y media distancia. Han pasado 60 años desde entonces y Radnaa Tseren sigue corriendo. "Corro de 3 a 4 kilómetros todas las mañanas", decía el pasado año en una recepción con el presidente de Mongolia, Ukhnaagiin Khürelsükh antes de proclamarse campeón del mundo Máster de 800 metros, en Florida. Pero Tseren no ha perdido velocidad y también disputa pruebas más explosivas, en las que igualmente sube al podio. Así, a sus 92 años, se ha proclamado campeón del mundo Máster de 100 metros en el evento de la categoría, que se está disputando en Daegu, tras ganar la final con un tiempo de 18.29, con +0.5 m/s de viento a favor. Lo hizo en la categoría de más de 90 años.

articles.title: 'Everyone wants to play cricket': Experts dissect Pakistan's decline in hockey after poor World Cup
articles.summary: Hockey News: Pakistanâs poor showing at the ongoing Hockey World Cup has left former players deeply concerned about the state of the sport. The four-time champions.
articles.body: Pakistanâs poor showing at the ongoing Hockey World Cup has left former players deeply concerned about the state of the sport. The four-time champions have now gone 32 years without winning the title and were knocked out of the competition after another disappointing campaign.They will now play South Africa in the classification match for 11th place.Former internationals believe Pakistan hockey urgently needs young talent and better results to regain public interest. They also feel cricketâs growing dominance in the country is partly linked to hockeyâs decline.Asian Games the immediate priorityThe Pakistan Hockey Federation has announced plans for a new hockey league and efforts to promote the sport in schools. However, former players believe the national teamâs immediate focus should be the Asian Games in Japan next month.Former Olympian Wasim Feroze said success against strong Asian teams could help restore confidence in Pakistan hockey."This hockey league and all is fine in the long run but right now Pakistan hockey needs an injection (of fresh blood) which will only come if we do well in the Asian Games against India, Malaysia, Japan, China, Korea and other sides,â said former Olympian Wasim Feroze, as quoted by news agency PTI.He warned that without better results, youngsters could continue moving away from hockey."Everyone wants to play cricket and we are not getting enough talent from the grassroots level,â he added.Former players question Pakistan's hockey systemFormer international Ahmed Alam believes Pakistan must find out why the team continues to struggle against European and SENA nations, including South Africa, England, New Zealand and Australia."Even against Japan, we've struggled. You look at the FIH Pro League where we lost all our matches against the European and SENA teams, and it is obvious Pakistan hockey has fallen way behind other countries,â he said.Pakistan finished ninth and last in the recent Pro League. Alam pointed to India as the only Asian team consistently competing with the leading European sides, Australia and New Zealand, crediting its stronger hockey structure.Former great Rasheed-ul-Hasan also expressed disappointment that Pakistan and India, once dominant forces in world hockey, both missed the World Cup semifinals.âIt hurts to see this but we have only ourselves to blame for allowing the European nations in the FIH to change rules to their advantage and then exploiting the changed scenario with their aggressive and fast style of play," he added.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Habrá duelo entre Ingebrigtsen y Kerr en el 1.500 del Ultimate de Budapest
articles.standfirst: Ambos atletas volverá a coincidir en una carrera... dos años después
articles.summary: Ambos atletas volverá a coincidir en una carrera... dos años después
articles.body: Habrá duelo entre Josh Kerr y Jakob Ingebrigtsen en el 1.500... dos años después. Será en el World Athletics Ultimate Championship, la nueva competición que se disputará en Budapest del 11 al 13 de septiembre. Para ello World Athletics ha contravenido sus propias normas, ya que solo podía conceder una invitación excepcional por disciplina y en este caso ha otorgado dos. Ambos atletas se medirán por primera vez desde la Liga de Diamante de Zúrich de 2024. El noruego, que sí tenía invitación automática para los 5000 metros como vigente campeón olímpico de la prueba, competirá en ambas distancias.  Tras sumar en Birmingham su cuarto oro continental consecutivo, en una temporada en la que apenas ha competido por los problemas físicos que arrastraba, Ingebrigtsen criticó la ausencia del británico en la cita continental, pese a que batió el récord del mundo de la milla y compitió en los Juegos de la Commonwealth. “Tenemos estos campeonatos por una razón y es para que los mejores atletas compitan”, dijo el noruego. “Creo que se está arruinando el deporte si no participamos”.  Por eso, Jakob aseguró con vistas al Ultimate que “me encanta competir y trato de hacerlo siempre que puedo”. Por su parte, Kerr afirmó que “esta temporada he tomado algunas decisiones que han dado mucho de qué hablar, pero siempre he querido demostrar mi valía en las carreras contra los mejores del mundo”. También el medallista de oro mundial y olímpico Gianmarco Tamberi fue confirmado para la prueba de altura. El italiano ganó recientemente su cuarto título en el Campeonato Europeo, con una marca de 2,32 m en Birmingham.

articles.title: Olympic hero Alysa Liu to sit out figure skating season before 2027 return
articles.summary: Olympic champion Alysa Liu will sit out the 2026-27 figure skating season, taking another break from competition while continuing to train ahead of a planned...
articles.body:
Olympic champion Alysa Liu will sit out the 2026-27 figure skating season, taking another break from competition while continuing to train ahead of a planned return the following year.

The 21-year-old American announced her decision on social media , saying she wanted time to "recalibrate" and develop her skating away from the demands of competition.

"I always want to challenge myself in new ways, so my artistry and skating can evolve," Liu wrote. "It's important to me that my sport reflects my personal growth."

Liu told NBC Sports that she intends to continue working with her longtime Bay Area coaches, Phillip DiGuglielmo and Massimo Scali, with an emphasis on her "overall artistry, spins, jumps, everything".

"I really want to improve my skating, and I wanted to take the time to do that for myself and just to evolve," she said. "And then I'll be back after that is done."

The decision represents another unconventional turn in a career that has carried Liu from child prodigy to burnout, retirement and an unlikely return as world and Olympic champion.

Related: 'She is our hero': Oakland celebrates Alysa Liu after Olympics triumph

Liu became the youngest ever US women's champion aged 13, when her 4ft 6in frame left her too short to reach the top of the podium without help from the other medalists. But the relentless training and attention that accompanied her rapid ascent gradually drained her enthusiasm for the sport.

She retired at 16, only months after finishing sixth in her Olympic debut at the 2022 Beijing Games, and later described how comprehensively she had come to reject the life built around her skating.

"I really hated skating when I quit," Liu said in the run-up to the Milano Cortina Olympics. "I didn't care about competitions. I didn't care about places. I didn't care about skaters. I didn't care about my programs. I just wanted to get away."

Liu enrolled at UCLA, studied psychology and went hiking in the Himalayas with friends while discovering an identity beyond the rink. Her desire to skate returned unexpectedly during a ski trip to Lake Tahoe, where gliding down the mountain rekindled her love of movement.

She began skating once a week at public sessions in El Segundo, California, and found that the difficult jumps that had propelled her childhood rise had not entirely deserted her. Liu eventually decided to mount a comeback, but only with greater control over her career, including her music, costumes, diet and training schedule.

The results would no longer define the experience, she insisted. Her initial ambition was simply to make another Olympic team and use the sport as a form of self-expression.

That approach carried Liu to a surprise world championship in 2025, making her the first American woman to win the title since Kimmie Meissner in 2006. In February, she landed seven clean triple jumps to rise from third place after the short program and win the Olympic women's singles title in Milan .

The West Oakland native became the first American woman to claim the event since Sarah Hughes in 2002. She also won gold in the Olympic team competition .

"Really the only word that comes to mind when I think about my entire journey is grateful," Liu told NBC Sports. "I think the reason why it's been so fun is because I have my own agency. I really like to skate, and so that's why I skate."

Liu said she assessed her emotional and physical state earlier this summer and concluded that stepping away was the right choice. DiGuglielmo and Scali supported the decision.

"Logically and emotionally and physically, this just makes the most sense," she told NBC Sports. "I will miss seeing the international competitors at all the international competitions, but there will be more, so it's fine."

A rush of opportunities followed Liu's Olympic victory. Nearly 5,000 people turned out for a homecoming celebration in her honor, where Oakland mayor Barbara Lee presented her with a key to the city. She withdrew from the world championships in March, performed alongside her Olympic teammates on the Stars on Ice tour, attended Louis Vuitton's Paris Fashion Week show and wore the label to the Met Gala .

Liu had been scheduled to compete at Skate America from 13-15 November in Everett, Washington.

Liu said she assessed her emotional and physical state earlier this summer and concluded that stepping away was the right choice. DiGuglielmo and Scali supported the decision.

"Logically and emotionally and physically, this just makes the most sense," she told NBC Sports. "I will miss seeing the international competitors at all the international competitions, but there will be more, so it's fine."

A rush of opportunities followed Liu's Olympic victory. Nearly 5,000 people turned out for a homecoming celebration in her honor, where Oakland mayor Barbara Lee presented her with a key to the city. She withdrew from the world championships in March, performed alongside her Olympic teammates on the Stars on Ice tour, attended Louis Vuitton's Paris Fashion Week show and wore the label to the Met Gala .
Liu had been scheduled to compete at Skate America from 13-15 November in Everett, Washington.
